questions: Does the oval still finish 20/20 near 1.65 s at 0.7 kg, or does the extra mass slow the finish enough to matter?
Does steering oscillation on the oval fall below the baseline 0.15, which would confirm that mass damps the controller?
On the s-bend and slalom, does progress rise above 0.17 and 0.12, and at what lateral error does the first line loss start?

intent: Single-variable test against the iteration-0 baseline: raise mass from 0.6 to 0.7 kg and keep every other value identical. The aim is to test whether extra inertia damps the steering oscillation that rose when mass was lowered, which may help the s-bend and slalom. Expected: oval finish rate holds at about 20/20, oval steering oscillation at or below the baseline 0.15, and mean finish time a little above 1.65 s. If the oval falls, the 0.6 kg baseline is the final geometry.
learning: Iterations 1 to 9 show the baseline is a sharp optimum for every geometry lever tested singly or in combination. Mass is the last single lever left untested alone. If 0.7 kg holds the oval and damps oscillation, a further small mass increase is worth a check in the final iteration. If it does not, the final design should be the 0.6 kg baseline.
rationale: Race evidence across nine iterations points to a sharp local optimum at the iteration-0 baseline (0.6 kg, 0.12 m track, 0.03 m radius, five sensors at x = 0, +/-0.012, +/-0.024 m, y = 0.05 m, 12 mm footprint). Iteration 9 reproduced it exactly (score 356.57), so the platform is repeatable. It is the only design that finishes any track: 20/20 on the oval at about 1.65 s. Every change since has either collapsed the oval or cut its finish rate. That covers lead at y = 0.03 and 0.07 m, footprints of 8 and 16 mm, the wider +/-0.032 m array (iteration 7 showed the earlier bend gain was not real), body length 0.12 m (iteration 8), and the combined track, radius and mass change (iteration 1). The s-bend and slalom have never progressed beyond about 0.28 and 0.12, so no geometry tested so far fixes them. Final evaluation runs on an unseen track, so a robust platform matters more than a speculative gain. Mass is the one single-variable lever not yet tested alone. Iteration 2 showed that 0.5 kg with a wide array cut oval finishes to 15/20 and raised steering oscillation from 0.15 to 0.21, which suggests the lighter robot is under-damped. My hypothesis is that raising mass to 0.7 kg, with all else at baseline, adds inertia and damps the oscillation, which may help the bends. The cost is slower acceleration, but the oval has a large time margin (1.65 s against the 3 s limit). Expected result: oval finishes stay at or near 20/20 with steering oscillation at or below 0.15, and bend progress is equal or higher. If the oval falls, mass is confirmed as an oval-sensitive axis and the baseline (0.6 kg) becomes the final geometry.
